item.title: Three Ways Families Can Make Mental Health Problems Worse
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Three Ways Families Can Make Mental Health Problems Worse

How ordinary family dynamics can shape depression and psychosis.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Criticism, hostility, and emotional overinvolvement predict relapse across many mental health conditions.
  • These dynamics aren’t captured well by the adverse childhood experiences framework.
  • The solution isn’t to lay more shame and blame on families, but counseling and education.

In 1959, a sociologist named George Brown led a study of 156 men diagnosed with schizophrenia who had recently been discharged. Most went to live with family members: parents, spouses, siblings. A smaller group lived alone in rented rooms. Brown followed them for a year. He found that among those who lived with family, about one-third ended up in the hospital. Of those who lived alone, none did.

Source: Khezez/Pexels

More studies followed. Data from a 1976 study suggested that cutting back on time with a critical relative was roughly as protective as antipsychotic medication against relapse in schizophrenia.

A 1989 study showed that the single best predictor of relapse among patients who’d been hospitalized for depression was their response to the question, “How critical is your spouse of you?”

A 1998 meta-analysis found that a critical or overinvolved family was linked to poor outcomes for conditions as diverse as depression, bipolar disorder, and eating disorders.

What’s interesting is that these aren’t families you’d ordinarily deem “abusive.” The standard framework for assessing family dysfunction today, the adverse childhood experiences framework, doesn’t capture them. These studies examine lesser forms of dysfunction, what many of us would call “normal.”

I’m going to wager that you’ve never heard of this body of research. As a historian, I find that this raises an equally fascinating question: Why not?

Moving away from the family

In the 1960s, psychiatrists were quick to blame parents for mental illness, especially mothers. Schizophrenia was explained by a “schizophrenogenic mother,” autism by a “refrigerator mother.” But the more careful psychiatrists emphasized that the problem was never solely the mother, or solely the father, but the family dynamic that engulfed mother, father, and child.

By the late 1970s, however, parents of patients were tired of being told that their kids’ mental illness was their fault. This era led to the emergence of groups like the National Alliance for the Mentally Ill, founded in 1979 by two Wisconsin mothers whose sons had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.

Such groups promoted the emerging biological perspective that viewed mental illnesses as brain disorders. Historian Anne Harrington, in Mind Fixers (2019), documents the role such advocacy groups played in popularizing the biomedical view.

By the 1990s, the biomedical model was firmly established in the American psyche. Everything was now a chemical imbalance. Family dynamics seemed to be off the table for good.

Today, psychiatrists claim that they’ve moved away from narrow biological reductionism to accept a “biopsychosocial” model, one that explores the whole range of factors that create and sustain mental illness. You’d think the family would have been put back on the map. It wasn’t, with one partial exception.

Advocates of the biopsychosocial framework often use the adverse childhood experiences framework to assess family precursors to mental illness. But its entries center on extreme forms of trauma, abuse, and neglect. The lesser forms of family dysfunction that psychiatrists once sought to understand remain largely off the table.

Expressed emotion

To my knowledge, only one research tradition has kept the family in view from the 1950s to today: “expressed emotion” research. It has built a robust body of findings.

Its core finding, put at the most general level, is that high “expressed emotion” in families is a strong predictor of relapse in numerous illnesses, including schizophrenia, depression, bipolar disorder, and eating disorders. To break it down a bit more:

1. Criticism: When the family member expresses constant disapproval, or when they insinuate that the person is lazy or selfish.

2. Hostility: When the family member disparages the person for who they are, or when they believe that the person could “snap out of it.”

3. Emotional overinvolvement: When the family shows excessive concern for the person’s well-being, and when they convey the message that the person is “unable to cope” with the world.

A 1994 analysis of 25 studies, covering more than 1,300 patients around the world, found that the link between expressed emotion and relapse was “overwhelming.” More recent work, by researchers such as Preethi Premkumar, has extended these findings to people who have never been diagnosed with anything, showing that young adults with mild psychosis-like traits (“schizotypy”) see their relatives as more critical, and the feeling of being criticized goes along with depression and anger.

This isn’t about blame

As I know from my own experience, having a loved one with schizophrenia or other serious mental disorder can be overwhelming, taxing, and uncertain. It can create a mix of intense feelings like pity, guilt, and anger.

Proponents of expressed emotion research emphasize that the solution isn’t to lay more shame and blame on families, but counseling and education. Clinical practice guidelines universally recommend family counseling.

Can families cause mental illness? The jury’s still out. But they can sustain mental health crises and make them more likely to recur. That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t go home for the holidays. But it may help to be aware of how family dynamics can affect your mental health.

A version of this post also appears on my Substack.

item.title: The Unintended Consequences of Good Intentions
item.description:
Emotional Intelligence

The Unintended Consequences of Good Intentions

We can easily get absorbed in our own point of view and move into tunnel vision.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Our plans could affect others, but it helps to see the bigger picture first.
  • Our point of view can lead to unimagined, unwelcome consequences.
  • We need to step back from our emotions and think things through.
Source: Vetre / Envato Elements

I was intrigued to read a recent article about honeybees aggressively bumping bumblebees out of the way when they alit on the same flowers, mercilessly chasing them off.1

It is a story of unintended consequences. Apparently, the number of registered beekeepers more than doubled between 2010 and 2025, following campaigns encouraging us to get involved in saving endangered insects. Now it seems that this growth in honeybees is having harmful, unforeseen effects on other wild pollinators.1

It happens so often, doesn’t it? Someone, often a politician, presents what seems a commonsense or creative idea to better a bad situation, then someone else calmly points out all the downsides that just haven’t been thought of.

We are so focused on whatever has our attention that we don’t see the big picture, leaving us in tunnel vision.

It is something that human givens therapists stay alert to at all times. When our clients focus on a particular view or sense of understanding, we can stay neutral, stand back, and bring attention to elements that they cannot see.

For instance, a client once consulted me about her plan to write a will leaving her worldly goods to just two of her three adult children. She loved them all equally and, on the face of it, her plan seemed logical. Her elder daughter had a lucrative job in finance while her younger daughter was a struggling actor and her son a struggling musician. I pointed out that while her plan made monetary sense, she wasn’t taking into account the potential emotional meaning of leaving money in a will.

Screenwriter, TV producer and novelist Daisy Goodwin has written about this. With her highly successful TV career, she had no financial worries and could accept that her siblings had greater need of the proceeds of their mother’s estate when she died. Her mother left Daisy just a small cash sum and some personal items and wrote in her will, “I leave my daughter Daisy out of the estate not because I love her any less but because I think she has less need of it.”

Daisy’s response? “But, and here’s the rub, although I know in my head that my mother’s will is fair, in my heart I feel left out. I love my siblings dearly, and I don’t begrudge them the money; I can understand they need it more than I do, but all the same I feel rejected. I am pretty sure that this was not my mother’s intention; she was trying to do the right thing as she saw it, but the result left me, a decade later, still trying to fight the feeling that she left me out of her will because she loved me less.”2

It is a good example of seeing just part of the picture and thinking others will view things as we do. Often, in such cases, what is conceived in generosity ends up causing unforeseen rifts in the family.

Michael was devastated when a presentation he had spent his personal time on was rejected without explanation. He had had “a revolutionary idea” that, he believed, would reposition the company in a way that would drive a host of new clients to them. He expected his bosses to be as excited as he was and arranged a meeting with the chief executive officer and second-in-command to demonstrate his vision in a dramatic video, packed with punch.

To his astonishment, his presentation was met with silence. Then he was politely thanked and told that “they would think about it.” Eventually, he received an email saying the company would not be pursuing his idea.

What Michael had entirely ignored in his single-minded focus on his vision were perspectives other than his own. His bosses felt undermined, and that the current approach, which they had masterminded, was being disrespected. Instead of taking into account their need for a sense of status and achievement, he had ridden roughshod over their ideas, expecting them to receive this gladly. The irony is that they probably all lost out. It was a honeybee manoeuvre, with no good outcome for anyone, when, correctly thought through and introduced gradually, outcomes might have been very different.

When we want to bring about change, we may have only the best of intentions. But we have to bring others with us, including critics or those who may be affected in ways that they don’t initially like. Putting ourselves in others’ shoes and foreseeing unwanted outcomes remain the unmissable first steps in all such circumstances.

item.title: 5 Things We’re Saying No to This Holiday Season
item.description:
Family Dynamics

5 Things We’re Saying No to This Holiday Season

What to do when family expectations take the joy out of the holidays.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Saying no to a holiday obligation can make room for something you’ll actually look forward to.
  • You can feel guilty about declining a family invitation and still make the right decision for yourself.
  • If the holidays feel harder this year, share the work or simplify the plans.
  • Keep traditions that bring you comfort and give yourself permission to change the ones that feel too hard.

Before you say yes this holiday season, ask yourself what you’re saying yes to. Consider the feelings that come up for you when you think about it. Is it excitement about seeing the people you love? Is it dread at the anticipation of planning, conflict, or grief? For some, it’s all of the above.

Recent polls find that nearly 9 in 10 (89%) U.S. adults report holiday stressors (APA, 2023). Tensions arise due to finances, family conflict, grief, and other factors. Stress takes away from the pleasurable aspects of the season, which should include reconnection and rest.

Sometimes that is easier said than done. Here are 5 things we're saying no to this holiday season and strategies to achieve the happy holidays we deserve.

"No, thank you" notecard at a holiday place setting
Source: AI generated

1. Guilt-tripped gatherings

Sometimes that family holiday announcement sounds like a demand rather than an invitation. “Dinner is at 4 pm sharp. See you there!” Everyone assumes you’ll be there, and no one asks questions. They don’t ask if you can take time off work, afford the trip, or have other plans. You feel obligated to attend despite any barriers you are facing.

Almost no one will tell you that you are allowed to consider your own needs before you RSVP yes. Ask yourself whether you have the time, energy, and money to participate this year. If the answer is no, it’s alright. Your family may be disappointed, and you may feel a little guilty, but it’s worth asking which will weigh on you more: the guilt of saying no or the cost of saying yes.

2. Disguised disrespect

In toxic families, it’s the once-over as soon as you enter the room. Before you’ve even had a chance to sit down, someone has made a joke about your weight or graying hair, offered a backhanded compliment about the dish you contributed, or slipped in a dig about your personal life.

You may feel hurt, sad, or even angry, and you don’t have to ignore those feelings to preserve the holiday spirit. You can be silent and stone-faced to let the “joke” fall flat. You might excuse yourself and regroup in another room. If you want to address it directly and call out the hidden meaning, you can say, “That felt like a dig,” or ask, “What do you mean by that?” What you don’t have to do is tolerate disrespect.

3. Overspending to prove your love

When you want everyone to feel loved, it’s easy to slip into spending more than you intended. If you’ve ever hosted a large family gathering, you know how quickly the groceries and gifts add up. And if you’re the one who hosts every year, it can feel like the work and the bill are yours by default.

Before you do anything, set a budget. Then share the work in ways that play into everyone’s strengths. Maybe enlist the nephew who can roast meat or the cousin who loves to bake, and assign cleanup to the one you prefer to stay out of the kitchen. Suggest rotating hosting duties. Do a gift exchange rather than buying individual gifts for everyone. You can show your love to your family with limits.

4. Burning out in the name of duty

In some families, playing the dutiful daughter (or son) means everyone assumes you’ll make the holidays happen. Often it’s the family matriarch or the eldest daughter who initiates the first call about the holiday plans and is the one still in the kitchen long after everyone else has gone home. She is the family “glue” who keeps track of the invites, remembers who can’t eat what, and figures out where to seat the relatives who aren’t speaking. By the time the holiday arrives, she’s too tired to enjoy the fruits of her labor.

If that sounds like you, name it. People who have never hosted may not realize all of the hidden effort that goes into an event. Bring it to their attention. Set limits on what you will do and ask for help, but don’t micromanage. If the person assigned to bring the rolls forgets, skip the rolls this year. If no one steps up, step back anyway. Plan a smaller, more intimate gathering that won’t leave you frazzled at the end of it.

5. Denying our grief

The holidays aren’t the same after you’ve lost a loved one, and the first holiday season after a loss can be especially difficult. Family traditions may be upended. The person who always hosted and made everyone’s favorite dish is gone. Tensions that surface after the loss may still be hanging in the air.

Take a moment to evaluate your feelings. Ask yourself what you feel up to this year. Maybe it’s not the year to take on hosting duties, or perhaps you stop by for dessert rather than staying the entire day. You can choose to honor your loved one by retaining old traditions or step into the next chapter with new traditions in their memory. You can miss someone deeply and still make room for moments of joy this holiday season.

It might seem strange that saying no could be the start of a happy holiday. The beauty is that you get to decide what a happy holiday looks like for you, and that it can change from year to year. Ask yourself what would make the holidays feel good to you this year and do it.

item.title: The Gift That Keeps on Giving
item.description:
Altruism

The Gift That Keeps on Giving

It’s the small, simple things we do that can mean the most to others.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • It's easier than we think to make an impact on others.
  • Small acts of kindness and support leave lasting impressions.
  • Helping others is linked to positive well-being for the giver, not just the recipient.

I was running out to grab a cup of coffee and asked my co-worker if I could grab one for her. No biggie, just a common courtesy. I literally didn’t even go out of my way. But when I returned, she couldn't have been more grateful. Sometimes when we do small, simple things, we realize later how much they meant to others.

It could be something like a thoughtful message or a quick check-in where we take a few minutes to listen.

The thing is, we often underestimate the impact of these simple gestures. We are all so busy these days, caught up in daily responsibilities and checking all the boxes to complete everything on our list, that we tend to forget how much we can effortlessly offer to others.

Of course, in this fast-paced world, we are always striving for more from life. And, at the same time, it's important to pause and recognize what we have and how it can be shared with those around us.

Even the Small Things Truly Make a Big Difference

Just take a moment to think about some of the people who make a difference in your life. Perhaps it was that friend who checked in on you during a difficult time or a supervisor who encouraged you. They may not have given their generosity much thought, but I bet you remember how it made you feel, right?

Let me share with you a research study that supports this idea. A 2023 study in the Journal of Experimental Psychology found that people frequently underestimate how positive acts of kindness impact others. In one study, participants who gave strangers hot chocolate thought the recipients would be happy, but in reality, the recipients were incredibly grateful for the gesture.

Science Says That Giving Matters to Us Too

Generativity, a concept developed by psychologist Erik Erikson, describes how a person wants to contribute to the lives of others and make a difference for future generations. This is evidenced in the things that we do, like mentoring others, supporting a friend or family member, or sharing lessons.

It’s important to mention that the research demonstrates a strong connection between helping people and well-being. In 2020, Psychological Bulletin published a meta-analysis of more than 200 studies and found a consistent relationship between helping people and positive well-being.

It’s important to mention that giving to others doesn't mean we are neglecting our needs. It just means that we are also helping one another build relationships. And the research also shows that a sense of connection really matters.

What Can We Offer Others?

Sadly, we are often so busy managing all that we have to do that we don't think about how we can support others.

So, let’s take a few minutes to reflect:

  • Who in my life would benefit from 15 minutes of me being present for them?
  • What have I recently learned that could help someone in my life?
  • Who in my life needs a little appreciation?
  • Is there someone in my life who might be struggling and needs a little support?

Which of these options could you incorporate into your schedule this week? (Choose just one.) You will both benefit if you reach out, offer a little encouragement, listen, or just let someone know they are on your mind. The point is that it doesn't have to be this big grand gesture. Small acts of kindness go a long way.

We’re Not Looking for Extraordinary

Life's most meaningful moments happen with people who took the time to listen, remember, or encourage, or helped us feel less alone. Don’t wait for more time or money, or until you've figured everything out, before you try to make a difference. Just start with where you are.

Take a moment and think about one small act of kindness that was bestowed upon you. How can you do the same for others?

item.title: How to Maneuver Generational Differences Over the Holidays
item.description:
Family Dynamics

How to Maneuver Generational Differences Over the Holidays

Navigating family friction and finding connection across the generations.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • During the holidays, aim for connection between the generations.
  • Discuss expectations and traditions before the event.
  • Choose shared activities that let all generations participate.
  • Respect boundaries and breaks.
Source: Nicole Michalou / Pexels

With the holidays yet again upon us, people will be setting their holiday gathering plans and preparing for an onslaught of multi-generational togetherness. When coming together for the holidays, the goal isn’t necessarily for everyone to think or celebrate alike; it’s to celebrate harmony and happiness while making room for the differences that you know may come with getting so many people of varying ages together in one room.

Here, we discuss how to make room at one’s table for generational differences while protecting the deep thread of connection that makes everyone family.

Different generations around one table

We’ve all experienced it. The sideways glances at the child who won’t eat their turkey. The sighs and stories about “Back in my day…” The admonishment to the teenager to “put your phone away.” The mom in the middle of it all who just wants a group photo of everyone before they dig in.

These are the sights and sounds of most holiday family gatherings. The younger generation has taken over the planning and organization of events, while the older generation sits in the wake of it all, wondering why anything had to change.

Even though the holidays bring together people who love one another, they can also bring friction. According to a 2023 American Psychological Association poll, 89% of U.S. adults reported holiday-related stress, and 22% identified the experience or anticipation of family conflict as a source of that stress.

However, generational differences don’t have to derail a holiday gathering. Once we learn to stop anticipating conflict and start remembering the reason we get together in the first place, we can begin looking forward to the fun stories, skill sharing, and memory-making that make the holidays so special.

Encourage curiosity, not conflict

It can be easy to get immediately annoyed when Grandpa starts talking about how they used to discipline kids or Great Aunt Margaret says that your stuffing was made incorrectly. Try to reframe statements before irritation or misunderstandings get out of control.

For example, instead of getting bothered when an older member of the family admonishes a child for being on their device, think about why they may be mentioning it. Perhaps they want to spend more time talking with the child, or maybe there are some cultural expectations around the holidays at play.

Researchers found that interactions and education can reduce or even eliminate ageism, which can be at play during multi-generational events. By teaching the younger generation about aging and helping them connect with older people, you can eliminate miscommunication, fear, and negative feelings.

Laying out expectations and boundaries can also be an effective way to help the holiday get-together go more smoothly between the generations. Prior to the event, invite the older generations into a conversation about plans. This way, there will be less chance of surprise or disappointment, and the older generation family members will feel like they are contributing.

Take care to ask about meaningful traditions in the family and choose a few to carry on while leaving room for something new. Discuss important topics like gift budgets, transportation, locations, and food options before the holidays so that there is less room for conflict.

Setting boundaries without a battle

Boundaries can sometimes sound like a dirty word to older generations, but they can still be important for intergenerational harmony during the holidays. First, distinguish between what you are willing to compromise on to keep the peace and a personal boundary that absolutely must be respected.

For example, letting Grandma tell stories about her childhood on the farm may not necessarily hurt anyone, but comments about your body, children declining a hug from a relative, or politics may be in need of some boundary-setting intervention. If boundaries that are important to you are repeatedly ignored, have a place you can go to take a break or a code word with your partner to signal that you need some help getting out of a conversation.

Aim for easier connection, not complete agreement on everything

When you get different generations of family together for the holiday, there is bound to be some friction. We live in increasingly divided times, and people may feel more comfortable around their family letting conflicting opinions fly. Holiday hosts should aim to connect the generations instead of steeling themselves for inevitable discourse.

One option may be to give the group of multi-generational party-goers something to do together. From making holiday cookies to sorting through old photographs or playing a group game, giving people something to do can help relieve the stress and discomfort that can often come along with generational divides.

The ultimate goal isn’t to resolve all differences and agree every step of the way (that’s likely impossible). Instead, families should make room for stories, laughter, and the kind of connection that’s only possible between people who know one another as well as family members do.

item.title: What to Buy This Black Friday If You Want to Be Happier
item.description:
Happiness

What to Buy This Black Friday If You Want to Be Happier

Research shows experiences bring more joy than things, and for longer.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • When asked which purchase made them happy, most people name an experience rather than a material item.
  • The happiness from an experience starts early: looking forward to it beats looking forward to a new item.
  • People waiting in line to buy experiences show better moods and behavior than those waiting to buy things.
  • Experiential gifts strengthen the bond between giver and recipient more than material gifts do.

When I teach positive psychology, a topic students are interested in is “What makes us happy?” What actions can we take to increase our experience of psychological well-being? With Black Friday here and many of us buying things we want or need, you can make smarter purchases for greater joy in life.

I’ll start with the bottom line: Research consistently shows that experiences make us much happier (and for longer) than material items (TV, sofa, a gadget).

Source: Dyunan / Pixabay

A few interesting examples:

  1. In a big survey of 12,000 participants (Van Boven and Gilovich, 2003), people were asked about a purchase that made them happy. The majority named an experience (rather than an item) as what brought them the most happiness. The researchers said it’s because experiences are more central to who we are (more aligned with our values and purpose) and strengthen our relationships.
  2. Anticipation matters too. People anticipating an experience (like a ski pass or a concert ticket) reported more happiness than those anticipating a material purchase. The happiness advantage of experiences begins even before the experience itself; the anticipation for it is already a gift (Kumar, Killingsworth and Gilovich, 2014).
  3. In that same study, the researchers also examined crowds waiting in line. People waiting to buy experiences were in better moods and behaved better than people waiting to buy things. If you've ever seen videos of shoppers waiting for a store to open on Black Friday, pushing past each other and sometimes even smashing windows, that is what waiting for things (items) can look like. You won’t see such events with people waiting in line to buy cinema tickets.
  4. A study paired strangers and had them talk for 15 minutes about either a possession (item) or an experience they had bought. Those who discussed possessions liked their partner less and were less interested in becoming friends than those who discussed experiences (Van Boven, Campbell, and Gilovich, 2010). And it makes perfect sense: I would love to hear someone’s passionate account of a rock concert they went to, but I would rather watch the paint peel off a wall than hear someone talk about the latest set of clothes or the new sofa they bought.

5. Chan and Mogilner (2016) ran four studies and found that experiential gifts strengthen the bond between giver and recipient more than material ones. The reason is emotional evocativeness: an experience triggers strong feelings when you recall it (remember that special vacation?) while the sofa won’t. It’s all about meaning.

When you are contemplating your next Black Friday purchases, consider these studies. Many other studies point the same way. Ask yourself what you really want from your purchases, and invest in the ones that bring you more happiness, meaning, and connection with yourself and others.

item.title: Zines Are a Great Tool for Learning
item.description:
Education

Zines Are a Great Tool for Learning

Making a mini-magazine helps learners connect ideas to their own experiences.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Zines turn learning into authorship and personal meaning-making.
  • Making a zine brings experience, identity, and culture into learning.
  • The process encourages reflection, interpretation, and deeper understanding.
  • Zines are low-cost, flexible, and easy to use at home, in classrooms, museums, and other learning spaces.

Post by April Ursula Fox, Ph.D.

A zine (pronounced “zeen”) is a little booklet or mini-magazine you make yourself, combining elements of a scrapbook, journal, collage, or a handmade book. You can write, draw, add photos, stickers, quotes, stories, or anything else you want to express. Everything is customizable, from page size and arrangement to colors, materials, and overall look and feel. Zines have a long history of giving people excluded from mainstream publishing a way to share their ideas, experiences, art, and perspectives. Today, zine-making is a worldwide culture, with makers sharing and trading their work at fairs, festivals, libraries, bookstores, and community spaces. The zine has become a cultural icon with a distinct history, community, and spirit of creative independence.

Why Use Zines for Learning?

Zine-making is a form of project-based learning and a student-centered way of learning through creating something meaningful. Project-based learning gives people an active role: they explore questions, solve problems, make choices, connect ideas, and apply what they are learning to real situations. Zines bring some especially useful qualities to that process. They give people many ways to work with an idea through writing, images, collage, humor, stories, symbols, personal experience, or cultural references, while also asking them to think about who will read or see the zine and how they want to communicate with that audience. The finished zine becomes something they can hold, share, discuss, and return to later. Across studies in classrooms and museums, zine-making has helped people connect course or exhibit content with their own experiences and interests, while giving them space to shape that learning into something distinctly their own.

What Happens Psychologically When Someone Makes a Zine?

Psychologically, making a zine brings together what a person notices, remembers, feels, experiences, questions, and connects while they are actively making something. As they revisit what they know, new information connects with prior experience and can reshape how they understand it. Putting ideas into words, images, and materials makes those ideas visible, giving the person something to reconsider and change. Thinking about an audience shapes how they communicate, while reflection can also turn inward toward identity and belief. Through this process, people build knowledge that feels meaningful and personal.

Zine-Making Supports Learning in Several Interconnected Ways

  1. Authorship and identity: People decide what matters, what to question, and how to communicate what they know. By reshaping information in their own way, they develop a sense of ownership over their knowledge and reflect on who they are and what they believe.
  2. Learning through experience: Memories, feelings, and lived experiences become part of learning as people draw, write, arrange, and make connections, sometimes discovering new meanings through the act of making.
  3. Making meaning through culture: People bring familiar stories, symbols, language, and cultural references into their zines, connecting new ideas to their everyday lives and sharing those meanings with others.
  4. Process over outcome: Much of the learning happens during creation, as people explore ideas, change their minds, make connections, and discover what they want to express. The thinking and discoveries along the way can matter more than how polished the finished zine looks.

Zine Example 1: Turning a Museum Visit Into Something Personal

In this zine, the maker transforms a museum visit into a reflection on love, connection, memory, and being alive. Using photographs from the visit, handwritten thoughts, museum materials, collage, thread, and a three-dimensional heart labeled “my core,” they connect dinosaurs, animals, ancient history, memory, and emotion through themes of love and interconnectedness. Museum content becomes part of a personal interpretation, helping the maker explore what the visit means to them and communicate that meaning to others.

Zine Example 1
Source: So Yeon Lee, Ph.D. / Used with permission

Zine Example 2: Making Course Ideas Your Own

In this zine, a student transforms educational psychology concepts into a personal explanation of learning. They use gears to represent thinking, a bell for behavior and conditioning, drawings of memory and motivation, and a child connecting ideas across the page. They also develop their own argument that creativity is a form of intelligence, extending the course material with a personal claim. By choosing how to connect and visually represent these concepts, the student creates both a reflection on their learning and an expression of how they understand education.

Zine Example 2
Source: So Yeon Lee, Ph.D. / Used with permission

Key Considerations for Making Zines at Home or in the Classroom

Zine-making is accessible almost anywhere, from homes and classrooms to museums and community spaces, using simple materials like paper, pens, magazines, photos, and stickers.

  1. As a parent: Offer your child a broad topic or question, let them choose how to express themselves, and encourage exploration through conversations about their ideas and choices.
  2. As an educator: Connect zine-making to a lesson, reading, experiment, or museum visit, inviting students to combine what they learn with personal experiences, images, stories, and cultural references.
  3. In either setting: Provide enough guidance to get started while leaving room for creativity and discovery. Encourage learners to explore the language of zines through words, images, colors, layouts, and materials, and discuss their choices to uncover insights beyond the finished work.

Anyone can make a zine, so give it a try and see what emerges!

April Ursula Fox, Ph.D. (UNLV), is an educational psychology teacher and researcher whose work explores learner agency, multimodal learning, and applied educational psychology across formal and informal learning environments.

item.title: Does Black Friday Make Everything Else Seem Expensive?
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

Does Black Friday Make Everything Else Seem Expensive?

How today's bargains can change what we're willing to pay tomorrow.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Black Friday discounts can change what we perceive to be a reasonable price long after the sales have ended.
  • Simply seeing a lower price can make us less willing to buy something at its original price
  • Retailers may inadvertently undermine the perceived value of their own products by offering heavy discounts.

There is something rather irritating about seeing a product heavily discounted during the Black Friday sales, only to see it back at full price a few days later. Before the sale, the original price might have seemed perfectly reasonable. But once the excitement of the sale has died down, it feels expensive, and paying the full price seems almost painful.

Black Friday discounts might do more than encourage us to spend money during the sales. They could also change our perception of value and how much we're willing to pay for things long after the bargains have disappeared.

Cheap is the new normal

When we buy something, we tend to think that we're making a rational judgment about whether it's worth the price. But how do we decide what something is actually worth?

One way is by comparing the asking price with what we've paid before or what we've seen the product selling for elsewhere. This gives us what is known as a reference price, a sort of benchmark we use to decide whether something seems expensive or cheap.

Over time, and after many repeated purchases, we become accustomed to paying a certain amount for a particular product. We accept that amount as its normal price, and it becomes what we expect to pay. But then Black Friday happens, which nowadays may last for a full month rather than one day, and that same product is suddenly available for considerably less.

Even though we know perfectly well that the discount is temporary, that lower price starts to influence what we think the product should cost. It can become a new reference point against which we judge future prices.

When the sale ends and the price returns to normal, the amount we have become used to paying no longer seems quite so reasonable. The deal has changed our perception of value.

When a bargain becomes a problem

When a discount changes what we think something is worth, it can also change whether we're willing to buy it at all.

Across three studies, Guo (2026) found that consumers who had seen an extremely low price were less willing to buy the same product later at a higher price than those who had seen a smaller discount. What was interesting was why they didn't want to buy it.

The discounts may have disappeared, but their psychological influence remains.
Source: Cottonbro studio / Pexels

Seeing the lower price reduced how much participants thought the product was worth. The prospect of paying the higher price also increased their anticipated regret. They expected to feel worse about buying something they knew had previously been priced for considerably less.

It didn't matter whether participants had previously bought the product at the cheaper price. Simply knowing it had once been available for less was enough to discourage a future purchase. We don't necessarily have to miss out on a bargain for it to change our perception of value, which the researcher called the postdiscount effect.

The findings raise an interesting question about Black Friday. If retailers spend weeks convincing us that their products are worth buying at heavily discounted prices, what happens when they expect us to start paying full price again?

The real cost of a bargain

This is where Black Friday might become a problem for retailers themselves. Black Friday is designed to encourage us to buy more by making products temporarily cheaper. But in doing so, retailers may also be changing what we're willing to pay for those products in the future. They could be inadvertently teaching us that their products are worth less than they originally claimed.

The more accustomed we become to seeing discounts, the more we might begin questioning whether the full price is ever worth paying. Why buy something today when it might be cheaper again next month in the post-Christmas sales? Why pay the normal price when we've seen exactly how little a retailer was prepared to sell it for last week?

There's nothing wrong with taking advantage of a good Black Friday discount. You've made a sensible decision if you've been planning to buy something and find it cheaper. The problem is when we allow that temporary price to determine what we think something should cost long after the sales have finished.

That's the irony of Black Friday. Retailers spend much of November getting us excited and convincing us that we're going to get extraordinary value for our money. In doing so, they might also be convincing us that their products were never worth the original asking price.

They may have saved us money today, but they've made everything seem more expensive tomorrow.

item.title: Think Someone Envies You? Here’s Why You Might Be Wrong
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

Think Someone Envies You? Here’s Why You Might Be Wrong

How to build real connection this holiday season.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Everyone envies and envy can be useful.
  • Avoid diagnosing others' envy.
  • There's no facial expression for envy.
  • Try curious warmth instead.

As the holidays approach, you're likely to meet new people and socialize with colleagues and family you don't normally see the rest of the year.

In such settings, you're also more likely to come into situations where you sense a bit of "healthy competition." Turkey Trot, anyone? You may also interact with people playing the "one-up" game, where someone shares a more intense version of the story or situation you just shared.

Envy can be awkward at a holiday work party, but doesn't have to be.
Source: Antenna / Unsplash

Whenever people gather, we're assessing and comparing. Everyone does it. It's natural. It helps us understand how we fit in and get cues on how to behave.

Envy not only can occur, but it can also help you navigate these times...though not in the way most people expect.

A Common Envy Mistake that Hinders Interactions

When some people discover I've written a book on envy, but they are not yet aware of its contents, they will tell me, "I don't feel envy, but I know a lot of people who do." They will then proceed to tell me about the people who envy them.

They don't know that I believe that everyone envies. It is a universal emotion. Unpleasant, yes, but not necessarily a harmful one.

I get it. In this culture where envy is often seen as a deadly sin, it's hard to admit feeling envy.

But not acknowledging one's own envy is unfortunate because you miss out on all that envy can reveal to you. However, that isn't the mistake I want to focus on here. I believe the bigger mistake is to assume that you know when someone else is feeling envy.

Two Reasons Diagnosing Others' Envy Backfires

First, we can't be certain it is envy they are feeling. Not only is it impossible to read minds, but we also can't reliably detect envy from their faces. As envy researcher Jens Lange told me, "If there were [a unique envy facial expression], we would likely suppress it."

Second, when we ascribe envy to someone else, we create an artificial barrier. We make a negative judgment about their character and lower their status to elevate ourselves. Not even conscious of this, we begin to operate on the false assumption and the distance we've created. It subtly impacts our interactions and our behaviors.

So what do we do?

Two Alternatives: Adopt a Warm Curiosity

First, adopt a curious mindset. It's harder to stop your mind from thinking of something than it is to suggest something new to consider. So, instead of saying, "Don't judge or make assumptions," try, "I don't know their story." Remind yourself that you don't know what happened in their past, what just happened moments ago, what their circumstances are, or what their mood is.

Second, dial up the warmth. Amy Cuddy, Susan Fiske, and Peter Glick's research revealed that when people encounter one another, they ask two questions: "Does this person want to harm or help me?" and "Is this person capable of following through with their threat or assistance?" They found that people tend to be envied when they are not warm but competent. So, if it is true that you're envied, more reason to approach with warmth.

During your year-end holiday festivities, try combining these two concepts and adopt a "warm curiosity."

  • Ask open-ended questions about what you are genuinely curious about.
  • Look for warmth and competence in others and provide a specific compliment.
  • Notice your own pang of envy and see if there are opportunities to express it as a compliment or question.

You may walk away learning unexpected reasons why you like someone you didn't before.

item.title: I Didn't Get the “Letting Go” Memo
item.description:
Parenting

I Didn't Get the “Letting Go” Memo

Personal Perspective: Mothering and letting go feel like a contradiction.

Posted November 25, 2026

I never got a specific memo about how to let go of my children. My parents, as Australians, were more open to this idea than the European parents of many of my contemporaries, most of whom had recently endured the trauma of the holocaust. But even with a different cultural background, I've felt that mothering and letting go is, on so many levels, a contradiction in terms. Mothers receive an intuitive message: You are meant to stay close to your children, to protect them, and to look after them. We assume this means always.

Well no.

There is a well-worn path of letting go, which surprisingly begins when a child is a few hours old. Lisa Baraitser1 opened my mind to this in her description of the newborn falling asleep. It describes the mother’s response, her feelings and tears as she realizes that her infant’s “first sleeps” hold a deeper meaning as he/she goes “away on their own for the first time.” It’s almost like a jolt, an awareness for the mother that her infant, a mere few hours old, drifts in sleep to a place that she isn’t part of. In the full swing of post-birth, we aren’t really tuned into receiving this message.

This realization would have helped me. It would have informed my understanding of mothering: that one’s child, even at a few hours old, is a separate being. It's a startling and humbling recognition that, as mothers, we don't own our children; we are “there to be left,” as Erna Furman2 puts it.

We get these messages continually from our children. The child crawls away from us to experience the world, then walks, then goes to preschool. But for the first 11 or so years, we are the ultimate hands-on caregivers. We feed, rock, and change our infants. When they are toddlers and young children, we kiss their skinned knees, and we are at their service all day and during the night to calm their nightmares and their sore tummies. To them, mom is the person who knows how to fix things—everything. We are their person.

This changes when our adolescent teenager surfaces. We become sparring partners, and if we are lucky, we get more than a contemptuous look or that stare. We return to nights of interrupted sleep, as we stay awake all hours waiting for them to come home. We spend a lot of time reflecting on and talking about what’s gotten hold of our child. Why is there no conversation? Why are they so abrupt and rude? Why is it all about their friends? It’s so difficult to reframe this as a process of healthy separation, a letting go, as they wear us out in a new way— with emotional exhaustion. Those of us who want to hold onto the earlier status quo are in trouble.

The teenage years give us pause for thought. How do we receive the message to back off, that we need to let go? One of the wisest comments that I ever heard about this stage is that a child is like this because he/she can be, because he/she has a mom who can bear it. The child intuits this through continual testing. It’s all part of the separation. It requires us to hold onto the sides of the roller coaster driven by our child, to stay on board and go with it while insisting on some guardrails, believing that our child will return to us one day, albeit in a different form.

Then, as our children approach late teens and early 20s, there are new challenges and shifts as they hopefully enter the workforce, continue their education, train for a trade or technical career, or go out on his/her own. We become more like roommates on different programs as we navigate home life with another adult. Or they leave home.

The next stage may include our child partnering, and the cycle begins again with their own children. Our next lesson is that it's their turn to make their own family. Are we able to watch and learn with curiosity and gratitude?

As we look back at our mothering, it’s clear that one of the most important parts of mothering is to intuit when to let go and how: to know that each child is different, and to ask ourselves whether we've been adaptive, accepting, and understanding enough. Have we tried to hold on too long or let them go too soon? Have we used guilt, been a victim, or judged them openly and harshly? Have we encouraged our child at each stage to learn their own place in the world?

How do we get there? Letting go of one’s children is an art form. It takes sensitivity, a lack of ego, and not putting ourselves first.

My work on ambivalence has guided my understanding of this. Mothering is full of contradictory feelings that can be difficult to bear, that often seize us at any one time, and also renew our love and give us the strength to separate.

Saying goodbye to our 4-year-old at preschool is a bittersweet love. We feel both fury that our 15-year-old arrives home at 4 am without calling and absolute love when he/she walks through the door in one piece. We feel pride and joy when we see our child commit to a partner, but also loss; they belong to someone else now. All of these feelings mean separation.

This is mothering.

Why didn’t someone tell me?

item.title: Every Choice Is a Loss: Why We Often Regret Lives Not Lived
item.description:
Philosophy

Every Choice Is a Loss: Why We Often Regret Lives Not Lived

Why choosing feels like losing: A look at Kierkegaard’s philosophy.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • We often think that the choices and decisions we did not make would have been better for us.
  • Kierkegaard, in the persona of "A," posited that life is inherently characterized by boredom and longing.
  • Neuroscience shows that our brains are the source of unrealized possibilities and regret.
  • Commitment to real life may reduce rumination about unlived lives.

Nurses often recount stories of patients near the end of their lives who express regrets about experiences they never had and paths they never took. They sometimes wonder whether choosing differently might have made them more satisfied with their lives. Regret is, to some extent, part of almost everyone's life. If we marry, we may eventually regret it; if we do not, we may remain alone and regret that too. If we emigrate, we may regret leaving; if we stay and endure our circumstances, we may regret that as well. Whether we remain in a tedious job or choose another, whether we speak our minds to those around us or keep silent, we may still end up regretting our choices.

Human Ennui and Regret

In the first part of Either/Or, Søren Kierkegaard—writing through the persona of a young man, "A"—posits that life is inherently characterized by boredom and that the choices we make are attempts to escape this state. We choose things that promise pleasure, yet such choices never lead to lasting joy or satisfaction; what is thrilling today may become mundane and tedious by tomorrow. Boredom inevitably returns, leaving us to lament the choices we made and wish we had chosen differently. To break this cycle of regret and boredom, "A" offers an intriguing proposal: much like farmers who rotate crops to prevent soil erosion, individuals should constantly alter their approach to life—avoiding fixation on any single experience—in order to mitigate boredom. Praising the character of Don Juan—the seductive, womanizing figure from Mozart’s opera—"A" champions the rejection of all commitments as a means to banish boredom and regret. In the same volume, Kierkegaard introduces another character, Johannes, who employs psychological tactics to seduce a young woman named Cordelia, gradually cultivating her affection. He uses strategies such as maintaining distance, employing silence, sowing doubt, and stirring the other person’s emotions—all of which he finds deeply pleasurable.

In the second part, Kierkegaard writes through another persona, Judge Wilhelm. He recommends that “A” choose an ethical and committed life. A significant portion of this section addresses marriage. Wilhelm argues that only a stable, committed relationship can prevent the initial fire of love and passion from quickly burning out, allowing it instead to endure. Through Wilhelm's voice, Kierkegaard writes that our choices shape our ultimate selves—an idea later further developed within existentialist philosophy. By employing pseudonymous characters, Kierkegaard deliberately avoids taking sides, leaving the conclusion to the reader. Ultimately, he presents choice and regret as fundamental components of human existence [1].

The Neuroscience of Regret

Now, we explore the neurological mechanisms underlying the persistent human experience of regret. In their book The Molecule of More, Lieberman and Long discuss two brain circuits—the mesolimbic and the mesocortical—both of which utilize dopamine as a neurotransmitter. The first circuit primarily drives "wanting," motivation, and the anticipation of a reward; it is not about the pleasure itself but rather the anticipated pleasure expected from a given stimulus. The second circuit activates top-down pathways for impulse control, enabling consideration of the future consequences of one's decisions and desires. From an evolutionary perspective, this capacity has allowed humans to transcend immediate, relatively simple responses and plan for the attainment of long-term goals. However, this simplified model of the reward system’s neurology suggests that repetition of a stimulus leads to a diminished reward—driven by a decline in dopamine levels and function within the mesolimbic system—thereby shifting attention and motivation toward new rewards [2].

Although the prefrontal cortex is primarily responsible for logical reasoning, evaluation, and behavioral regulation, certain regions within it also play a role in generating feelings of regret. A 2004 study revealed that individuals with damage to the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), unlike healthy controls, did not report experiencing regret or anticipating negative outcomes during a gambling task. Additionally, other brain areas, such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the hippocampus, contribute to the experience of regret by enabling the mental simulation of alternative, unlived scenarios [3].

Even the Thought of a Lost Reward Can Be Processed by the Brain

In an intriguing paper published in Science Advances in 2023, researchers examined the distinct roles of the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), the ventral striatum, and dopaminergic neurons in counterfactual thinking in monkeys. Their findings indicated that the brain can represent not only the reward actually received but also the value of a reward that could have been obtained through a different choice [4]. This suggests that, at times, the source of our regret is not an event that actually occurred in real life, but rather an event that never took place, yet one whose possibility the mind has retained. In effect, we may find ourselves mourning a life we ​​never lived.

In conclusion, the human brain is designed to anticipate the future outcomes of decisions we might have made and to compare those potential results with our current situation. While this capacity can aid in making better future choices, it can also foster a chronic sense of regret. This trait leads us to constantly evaluate our present circumstances against hypothetical alternatives—lamenting the paths we did not take. In the modern era, this inclination has been exacerbated by the rise of social media, which offers numerous opportunities for social comparison and exposes us to constant reminders of "alternative" lives. Observing the lives, homes, cities, and joys of others can trigger anxiety that we are perpetually falling behind.

Here, it helps to distinguish this phenomenon into two types: 1) Constructive Regret, which helps us recognize past mistakes and make better decisions moving forward; and 2) Ruminative Regret, which traps individuals in a cycle of constantly comparing their actual lives with hypothetical scenarios or the lives of others—without necessarily leading to any constructive action or decision. Since it is impossible to experience every life possibility or to know for certain whether a different choice would have been better, we can take the message of the second part of Either/Or to heart: By committing fully to our own lives, rather than constantly dwelling on lost possibilities, we can liberate ourselves from the anxiety and the wearying melancholy of regret.

item.title: Conformity, Individuality, and the Lawns of Levittown
item.description:
Conformity

Conformity, Individuality, and the Lawns of Levittown

Levittown shows the desire to express individuality and persistent conformity.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Levittown epitomized post-WWII conformity.
  • Levittown houses today express individual tastes.
  • Still, houses have lawns despite the environment hazards lawns pose.

Just a few miles from my home is historic Levittown, Long Island, where immediately after WWII, 4,000 acres of potato fields were plowed under to mass-produce more than 17,000 detached houses; many of these four-and-a-half-room homes were constructed in about two days.

Selling for less than $8,000 ($115,000 in 2024 dollars), each house came with a TV set and hi-fi. Buyers could choose a red, yellow, or blue house in one of three styles, in neighborhoods largely devoid of trees. This first modern suburb prompted historian Lewis Mumford to describe Levittown as “a uniform environment from which escape is impossible.”

A popular folksong tagged Levittown and other such developments as places of little boxes “made out of ticky tacky/And they all look the same.” No longer.

Drive through the area today, and it is nearly impossible to imagine the architectural conformity that it once was. What is striking about Levittown is that as houses aged, they became distinctive from one another and went decidedly upscale. They expanded upward and sideways. These four-and-a-half-room homes now are four- or five-bedroom houses with two baths. Barren landscapes are long gone. In 2024, Levittown houses were listed in the $700,000 range.

What Happened?

The sterile 1950s transformed into the turbulent '60s, with subsequent decades bringing tremendous social change in their wake. New generations moved in with new ideas; they had more money than did the returning war veterans. With time, Levittown’s appearance reflected the tastes of new homeowners.

Levittown reflects two contradictory impulses in human nature: The individuality impulse on the one hand, and conformity on the other. It is the universal desire to be recognized as a unique individual but at the same time desiring to be part of a group. The distinctiveness of the home displays this while adhering to the idealized standard of a suburban front lawn. You can drive for miles through Levittown—and almost every suburban neighborhood—and find that while the houses are no longer alike, not a single house has dispensed with grass lawns.

This would be a landscaping choice if it didn’t also mean that, to maintain the carpet-like appearance, the air is polluted with the fumes of mowers, the groundwater is poisoned with fertilizers (Long Island depends exclusively on its aquifer for its drinking water), and a din created by leaf blowers makes a quiet summer day around the house a rare event. Dispensing with lawns will probably have to be a policy decision, as there is only so much individuality that a person can express without feeling like an outsider. The change will have to come as an imposed municipal edict; not having a manicured lawn becomes a new enforced norm, where conformity becomes not having a grassy lawn.

item.title: Tasting Our Memories
item.description:
Memory

Tasting Our Memories

Personal Perspective: Why we strive to recreate perfect recipes.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Not every family recipe needs to be perfect to be meaningful.
  • Family recipes are more than food; they are connections to the people we've lost.
  • Holiday traditions carry memories, expectations, and sometimes a little culinary chaos.
  • Tastes change, traditions evolve, but the memories remain.

I’m standing in front of the fish counter at Market Basket, the grocery store chain that serves much of eastern Massachusetts. I scan the cooler for oysters. Shucked oysters, to be specific. It’s the day before Thanksgiving. I’m trying to recreate the menu of my youth. Those offerings included scalloped oysters, a recipe that my mother made every Thanksgiving and Christmas. Mom passed away in 2023. She never wrote down the recipe. She always followed the "handful of this" and a "pinch of that" school of cooking. She was masterful. I, on the other hand, celebrate the occasional culinary win, but more often than not, my successes are hit or miss—especially when it comes to the infrequent concocting of scalloped oysters.

Why do we try so hard, at this time of the year, to recreate the recipes from our past?

We are attempting to do more than recreate those dishes; we are trying to conjure the ghosts of those friends and family members who are no longer with us.

Roast the perfect turkey. Prepare the perfect pumpkin pie. Arrange an artistic nut tray. Make the perfect mashed potatoes with just enough lumps to know they’re homemade, but not so many that we ask, “Who cooked the potatoes?”

Some families carefully divvy the work among invited dinner guests. Auntie will handle the fresh cranberry relish, while Cousin brings the almond green bean casserole. Somehow, two people end up making the candied sweet potatoes, but one looks a little gray while the other is adorned with perfectly toasted mini-marshmallows. We will struggle to consume both. We don’t want to hurt anyone’s feelings.

Are we attempting to make Instagram-worthy dishes for the social media kudos? Or are we endeavoring to improve upon the butter-laden, sugary dishes of our youth? Remember that Uncle Robbie needs to watch his caloric intake after suffering a minor heart attack last spring. And Cousin Joanne is supposed to be watching her sugar since she started taking insulin to control her diabetes.

“It’s just one day,” we counter. “How bad could it be?”

But there are ethical considerations, too. Shannon’s new friend is vegan. Out of respect, we throw together a dairy-free lasagna. Is that really enough?

In-laws bring new traditions. My husband’s grandmother’s family favorite of orange ice befuddles our daughter-in-law’s family, but they agree to serve it every year. “We eat this first?” one asks. “But won’t the turkey get cold?” A question I’ve asked myself for almost fifty years. “Maybe this would be better served for the 4th of July!” someone says. And we all nod. And we never actually follow through.

New Orleanian author Amy Cyrex Sins mourned the absence of a recipe for Doberge cake after losing her treasured recipe file and her home after Hurricane Katrina ravaged Louisiana in August of 2005. While she suffered the obvious loss of possessions, it was the inability to recreate a favored family treat that continued to jab at her with the sharp barbs of loss, both physical and emotional. I remember sharing her essay with an honors college class many years ago. One student took it upon herself to make the dish. We New Englanders had no context to judge her success, but I know that I enjoyed a slice of cake that day. And I’ll never forget how she cut the cake by carving out a center circle and then cutting slices from the outside rim. A new tradition? Probably not. A new taste memory? Definitely.

But tasting our past and our memories encompasses so much more than carefully measuring and mixing ingredients.

When we attempt to recreate recipes from our childhoods and our pasts, we honor those cooks and chefs of our ancestors.

Vera, my maternal grandmother, was a terrible cook. I remember her making hamburgers and boiled potatoes. The patties were overcooked, the potatoes fork-mashed with butter and pepper. That was a staple meal served almost every night of the week! Grammy was a single mother, having been widowed at the age of nineteen. At the time, she was pregnant and had a two-year-old. Survival was critical. Tastes were secondary. And this was during the Great Depression.

One forgives a lack of herbs and spices when cheap ground beef and farm-raised spuds were often rationed between the extended family members of Canadian immigrants.

Psychotherapist and Relationship Expert Mary Pender Greene writes, “Remember that there are NO perfect holidays” (2009, p. 26). She suggests that the malaise of the holidays stems from “unrealistic expectations, which is often inspired by holiday marketing” (Greene, 2009, p. 29). Thank you, Martha Stewart.

One year, my husband received a 24-pound turkey as a bonus from his company. I calculated that the bird would take about 8 hours to roast. Just after 6 a.m., I popped the pale, featherless carcass into the oven. But at about 1 p.m., the fire alarm started to beep. Smoke filled the kitchen. I opened the oven door and orange flames licked at the stove front. My husband doused the fire with the white foam from a trusty fire extinguisher.

We didn’t have turkey that day. We had hamburgers. I think my elderly grandmother actually preferred the Thanksgiving dinner that day.

This year, I will once again attempt to make my mother’s scalloped oysters. I will be the only one eating them, as my husband and daughter eschew eating shellfish. But that just means more for me.

I hope that I swerve closer to the perfect scalloped oysters of my memories, but even if I miss that mark, I know that I continue to honor a long-held family tradition.

We strive to taste the memories of the past, but tastes do change. Ingredients become hard to find and obsolete. And that’s absolutely okay.

item.title: Preparing Kids for Their AI Future
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Preparing Kids for Their AI Future

The importance of developing AI skills to compete.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Artificial intelligence is here, and it's unknown how it will affect our children's futures.
  • The fundamentals of problem-solving and initiative are strong skills to learn.
  • AI makes finding information almost instantaneous. It's important children know how to do their own research.
  • Children need to learn the value of their own thoughts and beliefs to be able to better navigate their lives.

As you’ve most certainly seen on the news, artificial intelligence (AI) is here, and it’s in the process of changing our society. Depending on your point of view, AI seems to be either a blessing or a curse. Maybe both. While AI may help doctors cure diseases that have plagued us for centuries, it may also be an existential threat to our survival on the planet. The bottom line is, AI is here, and whether it’s the ultimate triumph of technology or the worst creation ever invented is yet to be seen.

While all of the differing reports on AI reverberate through the news cycle, it’s important for parents to know how AI can affect their children. For example, AI has aided in suicides by telling teens effective ways to harm themselves. Obviously, this is an extreme and major mistake. Hopefully, steps are being taken to stop that type of information from being dispensed in the future.

While these types of extreme examples get headlines and are acutely dangerous, there are other dangers that AI brings to children and their education that are not as widely publicized. For example, students can now use AI to do their homework or write their term papers. In the space of a few minutes, students can feed their assignment into AI and voila, out pops a well-written, factually sourced paper. If the student does a little tweaking, it may not be recognizable as AI, and the teacher may accept it as the student’s own work.

The Value of Responsibility

While cheating in school is not new, it’s never been this easy to game the system. While this can certainly be appealing to many students, the drawbacks of using AI to cheat carry real risks for their future. Beyond the information they are not learning within the paper they were supposed to write, they are also shirking responsibility. This can harm students by giving them a false sense of security in the present but damaging their ability to deliver what’s necessary in the future.

In any career, meeting deadlines is important. One of the ways in which we all learn to complete tasks within specific time frames is through school projects. If students don’t learn this, it can hold them back in whatever career they pursue. This is just one example of how AI’s seeming help can have long-lasting consequences.

AI is also going to make many jobs unnecessary. A student who doesn’t develop critical thinking skills, as well as specific areas of expertise, becomes an adult who is ripe for being replaced by AI. It seems that people who are able to think creatively, understand how to accomplish tasks efficiently, and learn to follow through on commitments are more likely to maintain careers.

What Can We Do to Help?

That’s why, as parents, it’s important that we talk with our children about the value of thinking for themselves. If they surrender all of their choices and individuality to AI, they’re likely to become little more than worker drones in perhaps the very near future. The more skilled and resourceful they are, along with building a work ethic that gives them self-esteem and self-confidence, the better prepared they are for the future.

The question becomes, what can we do to help? By sharing with our children the importance of learning and taking responsibility for their own futures, they can be better prepared to deal with whatever changes happen. By building up their self-image and confidence, they can see more possibilities for themselves and be more ready to face the challenges that arise in their lives.

It does not seem to be in the best interest of today’s youth to surrender to the ease of AI. By doing so, they may not be learning vital life lessons, which can undermine their futures. Our children need to know they still have a place in the world and can prepare themselves to thrive no matter what changes may occur.

item.title: Aesthetics Can Be a Strategy for Boosting Well-Being
item.description:
Creativity

Aesthetics Can Be a Strategy for Boosting Well-Being

Positive emotions from aesthetic experiences affect mood and promote well-being.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Aesthetic emotions play a crucial role in the processing and enjoyment of art.
  • Aesthetic experiences can have a meaningful impact on our mental health.
  • Aesthetic pleasure as an antidote to addiction.

Aesthetic experiences can arise from appreciating artworks—music, poetry, sculpture, the visual arts, nature, and the built environment. A distinctive feature of aesthetic experience is that it is not goal-directed but focused more on the activity itself. The focus is on the pleasure from doing something rather than achieving an ultimate personal goal.

Perception and interaction with art can evoke strong feelings, usually a sense of pleasure (Mastandrea, 2019). In the presence of beautiful things, we experience a broad range of feelings and emotions—fascination, awe, wonder, and admiration, chills, goosebumps, and crying. And being moved feels good (watching a joyful movie). For instance, most aesthetic perceptions of landscapes, natural scenes like sunrises and sunsets, tend to produce positive feelings of peacefulness, relaxation, and harmony.

Aesthetic emotions do not require us to act; they invite us to savor (Winner, 2019). Aesthetic emotions motivate prolonged and repeated experiences (you never get tired of watching a beautiful sunset). We also desire to possess aesthetically pleasing objects. Consumer-facing design and fashion largely focus on prompting consumer behaviors that drive purchasing decisions.

The Health and Well-Being Benefits

Aesthetic experiences can improve health and well-being in many ways. An aesthetic experience provides an escape from everyday practical life, and escaping one’s reality may improve mood. Art therapy and engagement with the arts are shown to reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety, ease pain, help people heal from trauma, protect against cognitive decline, and enhance social cohesion, among other benefits.

Aesthetic pleasure can be an antidote to addictive pleasure. Aesthetic pleasure differs from physical pleasures (alcohol, pornography, or gaming). We tire less quickly of artworks in one sitting than the pleasures we physically consume. The research on the role of aesthetic appreciation in addiction recovery is promising because it has the potential to provide a less costly treatment option.

There is increasing evidence that the aesthetic pleasure from art and music is no different in origin and function from the pleasure induced by food, drugs, and sex (Nadal and Skov, 2013). Art triggers the same pleasure as food or sex. For example, listening to highly pleasurable music can induce dopamine release in the same part of the brain as drugs of abuse. If the pleasure from art is no different than the pleasure from drugs, then one can substitute one for another (Christensen, 2017). If the high is the same, then getting it from a safer, more refined source should be even more obvious.

Education and Experience Shape Art Appreciation

However, one has to learn to see art. Art can seem intimidating to people with little experience of it. There’s no right way to respond to art. Aesthetic judgments are informed by a person’s background, emotions, and experiences. Education and culture profoundly influence our experience of art. We have no art module in the brain (Chaterjee, 2014). In contrast, we are genetically programmed to crave fat, salt, sugar, and so on.

We can nurture sensitivity (taste) for art with careful observation and education. To realize the benefits, Chatterjee (2014) suggests that we examine one work of art for 15 minutes, devoting five minutes to each of the three components of the aesthetic triad: What are its sensory features? What emotions does it evoke? What associations and knowledge does it stir up? This exercise may foster deeper engagement and create a more meaningful experience for participants.
