item.title: 6 Ways You Can Master Intentional 'Life-Crafting'
item.description:
Self-Help

6 Ways You Can Master Intentional 'Life-Crafting'

Living with intention can enable you to be the architect of your life.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Life-crafting builds meaning by aligning daily choices with personal values, goals, and resources.
  • Assigning different meaning to work and achievements can build meaning without changing circumstances.
  • Meaningful hobbies can build skills and confidence that fuel goals in other areas of life.
Source: Cottonbro studio / Pexels

In a study published in Frontiers in Psychology, researchers propose a model of “holistic life-crafting,” consisting of six strategies to create a more meaningful life. “Life-crafting” refers to the intentional and proactive process of designing one's life according to personal values, goals, and aspirations.

By intentionally balancing the demands life presents and leveraging available resources, individuals can reshape various facets of life that contribute to meaningful and satisfying living, fostering personal growth and well-being.

Here are six holistic life-crafting strategies to experience more meaning in life, according to the study.

1. Cognitive Crafting

Researchers describe cognitive crafting as a deliberate mindset shift in the way individuals perceive and derive meaning from various aspects of work and life.

Rather than physically changing tasks or circumstances, this strategy involves consciously shifting one’s perspective to initiate change. For instance, if an individual is working long hours and struggles to maintain work-life boundaries, they could begin by cultivating a significant non-work identity and daily practices to mentally disengage from work.

Further, if someone were to lack belief in their abilities, they can practice learning to highlight positive aspects of their work and everyday accomplishments over fretting about what they could not get done. Such alterations in one’s beliefs prompt changes in behavior, better emotional regulation, and a greater sense of control, mastery, and meaning in life.

2. Environmental Crafting

Another way to create meaningful change is by making external, physical changes to one’s work, home, or other life environments. Environmental crafting often involves setting clear boundaries between different areas of one’s life to prioritize and invest in personally meaningful goals and experiences.

Environmental crafting may include prioritizing time with loved ones or with oneself, engaging in meaningful hobbies, keeping work and living spaces separate, creating a home environment that promotes relaxation and creativity, or surrounding oneself with supportive, positive social connections.

3. Interest Crafting

Interest crafting refers to proactively seeking out, cultivating, and immersing oneself in enjoyable activities that hold personal significance and resonate with one's passions and interests.

Researchers suggest that engaging in meaningful activities facilitates the acquisition of new skills, competencies, and access to higher levels of creativity. Witnessing the tangible outcomes of one’s efforts also instills a sense of accomplishment and confidence while serving as a means of rejuvenation and inspiring goal pursuit in other areas of life.

4. Relational Crafting

Relational crafting refers to the intentional actions individuals take to maintain significant, fulfilling relationships in their lives. Through discernment, people can decide how to engage, when to engage, and with whom engagement brings the most value and joy. This encompasses not only nurturing positive and energizing relationships but effectively managing emotionally taxing connections.

Research shows that social connections are pivotal in creating and maintaining meaning and mental well-being. Relational crafting also subsumes the skill of navigating social dynamics, including conflict resolution and establishing boundaries essential for sustaining healthy relationships.

5. Skill Crafting

Skill crafting involves prioritizing skill development by seeking training opportunities, engaging in challenging projects, and capitalizing on one’s strengths to minimize setbacks.

Its essence lies in aligning one's capabilities with the demands and resources present in the environment. Researchers suggest that individuals who invest in skill crafting often experience heightened confidence, increased self-awareness, and a sense of capability.

6. Task Crafting

Task crafting refers to restructuring daily tasks or life elements in ways that resonate deeply with individuals’ inner drives and aspirations, finding meaning within activities by perceiving them as avenues for personal growth and embracing responsibilities that demand a broader spectrum of skills and competencies.

Researchers suggest that task crafting encourages a more purpose-driven and rewarding life. Individuals can engage in task-crafting by organizing their daily schedule to prioritize personally meaningful, energizing tasks such as going on a walk for their well-being and choosing to invest less time and energy in non-essential tasks such as checking social media excessively.

For instance, allocating specific time slots for checking and responding to emails or scrolling online creates a healthy time boundary between essential and non-essential tasks. This intentional restructuring of the day ensures that individuals invest their energy where it matters most.

Life crafting involves making conscious choices that lead to a more purposeful, balanced, and rewarding life. Individuals can start with introspection, which prompts them to confront limiting beliefs and explore alternative, more empowering perspectives. They must also ask themselves how different spaces in their lives can be altered to better support their needs and align with core values to create a life that is truly meaningful.

item.title: Gratitude Works and You Can Make It Work for You
item.description:
Gratitude

Gratitude Works and You Can Make It Work for You

The science behind gratitude and how to implement it in daily life.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Gratitude may help tamp down inflammation and reduce envy.
  • Gratitude has even been shown to improve athletic performance and reduce burnout.
  • What we focus on becomes our reality. When we are grateful, we create a happier, more peaceful state.

“Tis the time of year to be grateful (of course), and this might elicit many an eye roll at many Thanksgiving dinner tables. But there’s something to be said about gratitude’s ability to alter our mental and even physical well-being. Before we all tuck into our helpings of turkey this year, here are five surprising benefits gratitude confers, as well as some simple ways to be grateful—even when it feels antithetical to our current state of mind.

1. Gratitude can help us sleep better.

People who exhibit more dispositional gratitude have been shown to sleep better. This may be because gratitude, when compared with rumination, is a much more calming way to engage our minds as we wind down. Rumination can ratchet up our emotions and keep us wired. One study found that having individuals with a neuromuscular condition count their blessings each night for three weeks improved their sleep quantity and quality

2. Gratitude may reduce inflammation.

In a 2016 study, 70 patients with heart failure were randomly assigned either to journal about gratitude for eight weeks or to receive treatment as usual. The researchers found statistically significant reductions in inflammatory biomarkers among participants assigned to the gratitude journal condition. Other studies suggest that gratitude may tamp down inflammation by encouraging prosocial activities, like care and support giving, which can downregulate our body’s stress response.

3. Gratitude waters down envy.

Both dispositional gratitude and momentary (situational) gratitude can tamp down the green monster of envy, eliminating it altogether or at least morphing it from malicious to benign.

4. Gratitude may give athletes an edge.

A 2020 study assessed athletic performance across several sports and found that a gratitude workshop enhanced performance, improved stress management, and a more positive attitude towards training. Additional studies have found that gratitude can help protect athletes from burnout and increase motivation on and off the field as a function of hope.

5. Gratitude improves relationships.

An attitude of gratitude can make or break a marriage or long-term partnership. A 2012 study found that partners who were more appreciative of each other were more likely to respond to one another’s needs, demonstrate more commitment, and engage in more relationship maintenance behaviors, like initiating conflict resolution.

If you’re sold enough on gratitude by the above, here are some ways you can practice it in your everyday life. Even when things feel terrible.

List what isn’t awful.

On your morning commute, in your daily shower, or when you’re lying in bed trying to sleep, slowly tabulate as many things as you can in your life at present that are good, neutral, or at least not terrible. This is particularly important if you tend to hold grudges, ruminate over wrongs done to you, or generally focus on the negative. As you do this, you help unhook your attention from the things going wrong in your life and interrupt the rumination cycle.

Recall (in detail) three good things.

This classic gratitude exercise entails reflecting at the end of each day on three good things that happened from when you woke to when you sat down to journal or quietly reflect. Even on the worst days, this exercise prompts you to seek at least three good things amid the stress. These things needn’t be enormous or life-changing. They can be as simple as a pretty sunset, a strong cup of coffee, or that you have a roof over your head. Once you’ve come up with three good things, go back to the moments in which you experienced them and reflect in depth on what made them possible, who was involved, and how you felt during them.

Thank someone.

Write an email, letter, or record a voice or video note thanking someone who’s done something special for you or someone who just lets you be yourself. Better yet, arrange a "thank you" meet-up over coffee or an activity. The thanks doesn’t have to be for something huge, like saving you from a house fire (though this would certainly be something you would want to thank someone for profusely). It can be for something seemingly insignificant, like checking in on you during a busy time. Be detailed and specific in your thanks. Not just “thanks, that was cool.” But, “I so appreciated how you did _____ because _____; it makes me feel ______.” The more detailed we are in our gratitude, the more (positive) effect it has on the recipient and us.

If you genuinely struggle to see the good in everyday life or you’ve gone through a particularly long stretch of misery, it’s worth reaching out to a mental health professional. What we focus on becomes our reality, and many of us can get caught up in the bad news that seems to be coming at us from every corner of the internet or possibly even our social circles. A therapist can guide you through cognitive behavioral techniques to loosen negativity’s hold on your brain so that you can feel more regulated, safer, and connected—even in an era where that may seem like quite the stretch.

item.title: Falling, Your Body, and Your Brain
item.description:
Aging

Falling, Your Body, and Your Brain

A first fall doubles your risk of a second, making prevention a priority.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Aging slows the brain’s processing of sensory signals, making walking and balance less stable.
  • Shorter steps and weaker calf and hip muscles compound age-related balance changes.
  • Ongoing strength and balance work, plus a cane or walker when needed, can help prevent falls.
Source: Luskin International, with permission

As I approach 90, balance changes are occurring. As time passes, several brain and body changes make walking less stable.

Falls are the leading cause of injury for adults aged 65 and older, so everyone 65+ should develop increased falling awareness. Let’s think through it together.

Brain and Balance Changes That Develop With Aging

As we pass 65, there is a natural decline in the specific senses that send signals to the brain for mental and physical coordination. They begin to decrease. Walking requires brain-triggered nerve signals to and from muscles and joints, so as one ages, the brain’s ability to process these nerve signals diminishes. For example, with aging, gait slows, walking changes, and it becomes harder for the brain to sense body position in the surrounding space.

With aging, the brain's sensorimotor networks slowly diminish. It becomes more difficult to respond to changes in surroundings, and physical instability increases. By 90, using my own case as an example, step length has shortened, and my movements are less smooth than in the past. Muscle weakness in calves and hips compounds my brain changes.

With age, the brain's ability to integrate sensory changes makes walking less stable, increasing the risk of a fall. For some, the changes are subtle; for others, more pronounced. However, changes are normal, and they are real.

This happens to each of us at some point; the rate of decline is different for each of us. Yet, as noted, the CDC has identified 65 as a milestone year for particular attention.

In my case, I have fallen twice, and each fall caused a fracture. Statistically, women fall more than men, and a first fall doubles the risk of a second. So, my advice is to be realistic and make a plan to help avoid falling.

Strategies to Help You Avoid a Fall

To avoid falling, you should:

  • Become aware of your physical and mental changes.
  • Continuously work on strength and balance.
  • Monitor and make your home environment safer.
  • Identify and remove trip hazards, i.e., rugs and clutter.
  • Install grab bars, non-slip mats, and good lighting.
  • Use stable furniture for support when moving around.
  • Use a cane and/or walker for safety if you are unstable.
  • Always be alert and aware of your surrounding environment.

Common sense says that willingness to think about falling in the future is important as we age, and the best kind of falls are those we avoid by staying alert and paying attention.

item.title: In the Company of 92-Year-Olds
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

In the Company of 92-Year-Olds

Personal Perspective: Two nonagenarians demonstrate the delight of living well.

Posted November 25, 2026

Key points
  • Spending time with two nanogenarians showed how to age with verve and grace.
  • Each of them lives independently and are excellent company.

I recently visited a couple of 92-year-olds, one in New Jersey, the other in Florida. Both are spry, funny, and ready to die. But neither is in a big rush to do so.

Source: Oscar Salgado/Unsplash

New Jersey was our first stop. Anne and I met 25-plus years ago at a workshop she was co-leading in California and have stayed in touch since. Over the years, we attended a few workshops together, the most memorable of which was in Seattle, where we ditched a talk and laughed ourselves sick in the tiny dorm room we shared.

Today Anne lives in a one-bedroom apartment in a town across the river from New York City. She never had kids, and her few relatives live far away. She’d been introduced to Dave, my new(ish) fella, by phone a while back, but this was their first face-to-face. I caught a whiff of flirtatiousness during their phone meeting, which was quickly and delightfully confirmed in the flesh.

While she craves in-person contact, her social circles are deep and wide. She hosts online groups for issues related to aging, coaches writing, and is a podcast guest and webinar speaker.

I’ve traveled with Anne enough to have a decent sense of her natural flow. She’s more purposeful than she is slow, taking a leisurely pace with her morning ablutions. She also knows what she needs and when enough is enough.

One day, for example, she insisted we take her car and toodle up the Hudson River to see the autumn colors. Sitting in a vehicle most of the day wasn’t her idea of fun, so she stayed behind. She offered detailed directions and drew us a map. Upon our return, she plied us with questions about what we saw and what we did on our adventure. We played Rummikub after dinner. She beat the pants off us both, then kicked us out.

Tears were shed as we said our goodbyes. Anne and Dave put their hands on each other’s shoulders, declaring themselves sister and brother of the heart, then folded me into their tight embrace.

Source: Martin Sanchez/Unsplash

Then we boarded the train to Florida, where my 92-year-old friend Bob and his daughter picked us up at the station. He and I met over 30 years ago, when my ex and I hung out regularly with a pack of folks in rural Oregon.

After his much-adored wife died eight years ago, Bob relocated to be near family. I hadn’t seen him since, though we talk by phone every month or so. He lives independently in a three building highrise complex next to the sea. Everyone knows him.

Bob is an elegant host, and always makes others feel cared for. He and I picked up where we left off, seamlessly folding Dave into civil discussions of the upcoming election and a long list of outings Bob proposed. Our number-one choice was the Kennedy Space Center.

We three boarded a bus from the parking lot to the Apollo/Saturn V Center, located a few miles from the main Visitor Center. As we exited the bus, our driver suggested we step to the front of the line for our return trip so we could sit together and avoid having to walk to the back of the bus. Given how many miles we ended up covering on foot that day, it was a kind, but unnecessary accommodation.

Spry is Bob’s middle name. We traipsed through the entire campus, then he insisted we experience the Space Shuttle Vertical Motion Simulator, which recreates the experience of liftoff. We were shaken, squished, and elevated, each of us happy to have chosen less rigorous careers. A long day well spent.

What is it about these two that makes them so dear? In Anne's case, I think it boils down to her warmth and delight in knowing what makes another person who they are. She craves connection and makes it happen. Bob has a natural curiosity about the world around him and is a careful listener. That makes him a great conversationalist who draws others close. He lets you know you matter.

During our time together, these two nonagenarians showed us what it means to be warm, vital, and utterly companionable seniors. They’re both good drivers and mentally sharp. Neither complained about physical ailments nor expressed regret about how their lives had unfolded, including the tough stuff they’ve both endured. Rather, they celebrated our time together, our shared history, and the satisfaction of sharing their amazing lives.

I plan on visiting Anne again next spring, so our goodbyes felt temporary. Leaving Bob, however, we acknowledged this was likely our last time together in person. We hugged tearfully and agreed to connect on the other side.
